newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan party asks big price for Hashimoto coalition.
newsitem.headline: Japan party asks big price for Hashimoto coalition.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, struggling to secure a majority in Japan's hung parliament, ran into more trouble on Friday when his potential partners decided to seek a high price to form a coalition.

In last week's general elections, Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) ended up a dozen seats short of a majority in parliament's powerful Lower House, forcing the party to court coalition partners.
Hashimoto allies in the outgoing coalition, the Social Democrats, are again an ideal partner, since their strength would give a renewed LDP-led coalition command of both houses in parliament.
The conservative LDP holds 239 seats in the 500-member Lower House and 109 in the 252-member Upper House. The Social Democrats have 15 in the Lower House and 32 in the Upper House.

But on Friday, the Social Democrats said they would insist that the LDP agree on a platform including a strict ban on political donations from companies, which would be anathema to the LDP, with its close links to corporate Japan.
"The ban on donations from corporations will be an integral part of our policy proposal," a Social Democrat spokesman said.

The spokesman said the proposal, including other policy issues such as cutting back on bloated bureaucracy and putting the brakes on moves to draw up security guidelines with the United States, will be formally presented to the LDP in policy negotiations starting on Saturday.
The LDP, which has spent most of the past four decades in power, has been helped by political funds from big business, the farm vote and administrative support from bureaucrats.

For Hashimoto, accepting the Social Democrats' demands, especially the ban on corporate donations, would be political suicide. It would certainly incur the wrath of the LDP's powerful right wing, who put him in power in the first place. Hashimoto seeks re-election as LDP president next September.
Hashimoto may be forced to lead a weak, minority government which would mean that every piece of legislation, including key budget bills, could easily become bogged down.

Among the LDP's other possible partners, the fledgling Democratic Party, led by Yukio Hatoyama and Naoto Kan, who represent a younger generation of radical reformists, also said it was against corporate donations for political parties.
"As far as the Democratic Party is concerned, we will strive to put an end to this malpractice of corporate donations," Kan told a news conference on Friday.
Hatoyama has said his party should stay in the opposition benches to ensure its reformist voice is heard.
The Social Democrats' stance means the policy negotiations beginning on Saturday would be a drawn-out affair, parliamentary sources said.
The Social Democrats do not want to be seen as a weak party desperately seeking a share of power, while the LDP cannot afford to be seen as giving in too much to smaller parties, the sources said.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama has said the government intends to recovene parliament on November 7 to elect a new prime minister, giving the parties less than two weeks to negotiate.
The opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) holds only 156 seats in the powerful Lower House, which rules out any form of viable alliance excluding the LDP.

In any case, Shinshinto is rife with dissent -- the party expelled a member of parliament on Thursday for hinting at moves to lead a mass defection -- and is in no position to enter into any negotiations with its arch-rival LDP.
